title: Kwyst - Text Based Adventure Game
author: Uplipht
selftext:
Hey guys!

I’m building [Kwyst](https://www.kwyst.com) \- a daily challenge format-based text adventure game with an AI narrator that maps user choices to a story graph, and can create new nodes and branches for creative decisions.

My goal was to combine two things I love: written storytelling and games.

I went with a daily challenge format because I think a lot of modern AI-driven text adventure games end up being a prolonged battle of verbosity with a poorly constrained narrative structure. They generally aren’t accessible by wide audiences who don’t like the complexity of tracking stats, complex die roll mechanics, etc.

It’s still very much a work in progress - but it’s functional enough that I felt comfortable putting out my prod build for others to freely try and play.

The stories are hand-crafted by me every day - my own words, general narrative structure, interesting decisions and consequences, and “level” design. The AI then operates within the bounds of my world and dynamically constructs new narrative paths, judges and scores creativity of branches or decisions that I didn’t think of, and allows players to solve the problems and complete the challenge how they see fit.

As I grow more confidence in the narrative engine, i’ll continue to shift time and resources away from development to build more compelling narratives across multiple genres (right now i’m definitely trending more towards comedy in my first three daily challenges I have written)

Because I have a per-user token cost, access is limited to a set number of accounts while I finalize monetization setup and plans.

Would love feedback on the general structure, and any breaking issues you find in the narrative engine!

If you decide to play, you can report bugs or feedback to me here or at support@kwyst.com

You can find the game at [https://play.kwyst.com](https://play.kwyst.com)

Thanks!

replies.author: Uplipht
replies.body:
The dice roll is determined based off of a factor of riskiness, creativity, and resourcefulness.

Using something in your environment in a creative way that would have a low downside risk if it didn’t work would give you the most favorable dice roll requirement. This is the feature that right now is the least consistent and i’m testing a couple changes to the engine to improve it.

The cool part about the game (that I haven’t really been able to test super thoroughly because it requires a large user count) is that when you make a creative decision (something not already on the graph) - the story graph is updated so that when a user makes that same decision later they will get the same dice roll requirements you did. I’m trying to ensure fairness and consistency when you compare your run to someone else’s.

And when it updates or compares your action to the graph, it looks at your intention and actions (not just direct word matches so that “shove” and “push” don’t create separate nodes). Theoretically, two users making the same decisions and having the same luck on their dice rolls should get the same outcome. But one small change in your actions on one turn can have a butterfly effect to put you on a different trajectory.

The actual value of your dice roll is a server-generated random number.

Probably way more info than you wanted but thats the full explanation lol

comments.author: Halloween_Forever_
comments.body: Question, the game itself doesn't contain an llm right? I am very new to this, but i was considering a mystery solver with an llm being a backbone of sorts, then figured if i wanted to send it to anyone i would have to include the llm, or player would have to install one themselves. Just a little thing i was considering.

replies.author: Uplipht
replies.body:
Depends on how you want to host/offer it.

Mine uses a gateway and an API key that goes to my openAI subscription. I have overall limits and per-account token limits that I enforce server-side. The entire game structure is built around hitting a per-user, per-day token quota to ensure the app can be profitable.

If you’re writing a desktop app, you can just have a user provide their own API key in an environment variable or config file.

I would definitely be careful with any online service that provides an LLM interface that users can influence in any way - bad users can rob you blind (intentionally or unintentionally).

I work in security and over-engineered the protections on this app to feel comfortable offering it publicly, I wouldn’t advise someone who doesn’t understand security to build a web facing game with a user reachable LLM interface unless you turn on strict token budgets and are comfortable losing a little bit of money.
